subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Right now, as you read this, invisible pushes and pulls are acting on you. Gravity is holding you down onto your chair. The chair is pushing back up so that you do not sink through it. If a cool breeze from the Indian Ocean blows through the window, you can feel the air pushing gently against your skin. Every one of these pushes and pulls is a force, and this unit is all about forces and the way they make things move, stop, and change shape.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Distinguish between mass measured in kilograms (kg) and weight measured in newtons, noting that kilograms are used in everyday life
Recognise and use units of force, mass and weight and identify the direction in which forces act
Understand the notion of energy in movement
Recognise friction (including air resistance) as a force which can affect the speed at which objects move and which sometimes stops things moving

outcomes: Explain what a force is and describe forces as pushes or pulls that have both size and direction.
Name the main types of force: gravity, friction, air resistance, water resistance, and pushes and pulls from contact.
Explain the difference between mass (measured in kilograms) and weight (measured in newtons).
Calculate the weight of an object using the rule weight = mass x gravity.
Describe how friction helps us and how it slows us down, and compare friction on sandy and paved roads.
Explain balanced and unbalanced forces and predict whether an object will speed up, slow down, or stay the same.
Measure forces in newtons using a forcemeter you build yourself.
Calculate speed using the rule speed = distance / time.
Give real examples of forces from farming, fishing, sport, and travel in East Africa.
Here are the most important words in this unit. Keep coming back to this table whenever a word confuses you.

concepts.title: A Force Is a Push or a Pull
concepts.explanation:
Everything begins with one simple idea. A force is a push or a pull. That is it. When you push open a wooden door, you use a force. When you pull a bucket of water up from a well, you use a force. A force can never be seen with your eyes, but you can always see or feel what it does. Forces are like the wind: you do not see the wind itself, only the way it bends the acacia trees and fills the sail of a dhow.

Every force has two important features. The first is its size — how strong the push or pull is. Pushing a small child on a swing needs a gentle force; pushing a fully loaded donkey cart out of soft sand needs a much larger force. The second feature is its direction — which way the push or pull points. If you push a football to the left, it rolls left. If you push it forward, it rolls forward. Because forces have both size and direction, scientists draw them as arrows. A longer arrow means a bigger force, and the way the arrow points shows the direction of the force.

Some forces work only when two objects touch each other. These are contact forces. When you kick a ball, cut vegetables with a knife, or push a wheelbarrow, your object must touch the thing it moves. Other forces can act across a gap without touching. These are non-contact forces. Gravity is the most important non-contact force: the Earth pulls a mango down even though the Earth is not touching the mango. A magnet pulling a nail from a small distance is another non-contact force you may have seen.

Did You Know? A force is measured in a unit called the newton, written with a capital N. It is named after Sir Isaac Newton, an English scientist who lived over 300 years ago. The story says he began thinking about gravity after watching an apple fall from a tree — much like a mango falling in your own garden.
concepts.example: Forces can do several different jobs. A force can make a still object start moving, like a football that stays put until your foot strikes it. A force can make a moving object stop, like the brakes on a bicycle. A force can make something speed up or slow down, and it can make a moving object change direction, the way a defender in football can turn the ball aside with the side of his boot. Finally, a force can change the shape of an object: squeezing a piece of dough, stretching a rubber band, or bending a green twig all use forces to change shape.

concepts.title: Gravity, Mass, and Weight
concepts.explanation:
Hold a stone in your hand and let go. It drops straight down. Every single time, no matter where you stand, objects fall toward the ground. The force that pulls them down is gravity. Gravity is the pull between any two objects that have mass, but the Earth is so enormous that its gravity is the pull we notice most. Earth's gravity reaches out and pulls everything toward the centre of the planet. That is why a dropped mango falls down and never sideways or up.

To understand gravity properly, you must learn the difference between two words that people often mix up: mass and weight. They are not the same thing, and keeping them separate is one of the most important ideas in this whole unit.

Mass is the amount of matter — the amount of 'stuff' — inside an object. Mass is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). A bag of rice with a mass of 5 kg contains a certain amount of rice, and that amount never changes. Whether you carry that bag in Nairobi, on top of a mountain, or all the way to the Moon, it still contains exactly 5 kg of rice. Mass stays the same everywhere in the universe because the amount of stuff has not changed.

Weight is different. Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, and because it is a force, it is measured in newtons (N). Weight can change. On the Moon, gravity is much weaker than on Earth — only about one sixth as strong. So your 5 kg bag of rice would still have a mass of 5 kg on the Moon, but it would weigh far less because the Moon pulls on it more gently. Mass is about how much stuff there is; weight is about how hard gravity pulls on that stuff.

On Earth, there is a simple rule that connects mass and weight. For every 1 kilogram of mass, gravity pulls with a force of about 10 newtons. Scientists call this number the gravitational field strength, and on Earth it is about 10 newtons for every kilogram (written 10 N/kg). This gives us a very useful rule that you will use again and again:

Weight = mass x gravity, or in short, W = m x g, where g = 10 N/kg on Earth.

This rule lets you work out the weight of anything if you know its mass. It also explains why a bigger mass always weighs more: the more matter there is, the harder gravity pulls. A camel has a much greater mass than a chicken, so gravity pulls on the camel with a far greater force, and the camel weighs much more.

Let us practise the weight rule together, one careful step at a time. Read each example slowly and make sure you understand every line before moving on. Keep the rule in front of you: Weight = mass x gravity, and on Earth gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Amina buys a bag of rice with a mass of 5 kg in the market at Garissa. What is its weight on Earth?

Write down what you know. Mass m = 5 kg. Gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Write the answer with the correct unit. The weight of the rice is 50 newtons (50 N).

Notice that the mass is written in kilograms and the answer is written in newtons. Weight is always a force, so it is always measured in newtons, never in kilograms.

Hassan fills a plastic jerrycan with water. The full jerrycan has a mass of 20 kg. What is its weight?
concepts.example: This rule lets you work out the weight of anything if you know its mass. It also explains why a bigger mass always weighs more: the more matter there is, the harder gravity pulls. A camel has a much greater mass than a chicken, so gravity pulls on the camel with a far greater force, and the camel weighs much more.

concepts.title: Friction - The Force That Grips and Slows
concepts.explanation:
Push a wooden box across the floor and let go. It slides a little way and then stops. What made it stop? A force called friction. Friction is a force that appears whenever two surfaces rub against each other, and it always pushes against the direction of movement. When the box slides forward, friction pushes backward and slows it down until it stops.

Friction depends on how rough or smooth the surfaces are. Two rough surfaces rubbing together produce a large friction force. Two smooth surfaces produce much less. You can feel this difference under your own feet. Think about walking on a sandy road near the coast: the loose, gritty sand grips your sandals, and it takes real effort to drag your feet or push a cart through it. Now think about walking on a smooth paved road in the city: your feet slide along easily and a cart rolls with far less effort. The paved road has less friction than the sandy road.

Did You Know? Friction always turns movement energy into heat. Rub your two hands together quickly and you will feel them grow warm — that heat comes from friction. This is the same reason bicycle brakes and car tyres become hot after being used for a long time.

It is easy to think of friction as a nuisance because it slows things down and wears them out. But friction is often our friend. Without friction between your sandals and the ground, you could not walk at all — your feet would slip out from under you like they do on wet, slippery mud. Friction lets a footballer stop and turn quickly. Friction lets the wheels of a car grip the road instead of spinning uselessly. Friction lets you hold a pencil without it sliding out of your fingers. Whenever you need grip, friction is helping you.

At other times we want less friction. A fisherman greases the moving parts of his boat so they slide smoothly. Machine parts are oiled so they do not wear each other away. Race cars and even dhows are shaped to slip through air and water with as little resistance as possible. Learning when to increase friction and when to reduce it is a big part of engineering.
concepts.example: Push a wooden box across the floor and let go. It slides a little way and then stops. What made it stop? A force called friction. Friction is a force that appears whenever two surfaces rub against each other, and it always pushes against the direction of movement. When the box slides forward, friction pushes backward and slows it down until it stops.

concepts.title: Air Resistance and Water Resistance
concepts.explanation:
Air and water are all around us, and although they feel light and thin, they push back against anything that moves through them. Air resistance is a special kind of friction between a moving object and the air it pushes through. It is also called drag. The faster you move and the bigger your surface, the more air resistance you feel. Run fast on a windy day and you can feel the air pushing against your chest and face.

The clearest example of air resistance is a parachute. When a person jumps and opens a parachute, the wide sheet of cloth traps a huge amount of air beneath it. The air cannot rush out of the way quickly, so it pushes up hard against the parachute. This large upward air resistance balances much of the downward pull of gravity, so the person floats down gently and safely instead of falling fast. You can see the same idea when a light seed or a piece of paper drifts slowly to the ground while a stone drops straight down — the flat, light object catches far more air.

Water resistance works in the same way but in water. Anything that moves through water must push the water aside, and the water pushes back. A fisherman on the Indian Ocean feels water resistance every time he pulls a net through the sea. A swimmer feels it with every stroke. This is why fish have smooth, pointed, streamlined bodies: a streamlined shape lets water slide past easily, so the fish can move quickly using less effort. Boats and dhows are built with narrow, smooth hulls for exactly the same reason — to reduce water resistance and glide more easily across the waves.
concepts.example: Interestingly, the wind can also be a helpful pushing force rather than a resistance. When a dhow raises its sail on the Indian Ocean, the sailors are using the force of the wind to push the whole boat forward. Here the moving air is not slowing the boat down — it is providing the push that carries cargo and fishermen up and down the coast. The very same air that resists a running child can drive a heavy boat across the sea when it is caught in a sail. Forces depend on how we use them.

concepts.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
concepts.explanation:
Usually more than one force acts on an object at the same time. To predict what will happen, you must add up all the forces and see which way they win. This is where the ideas of balanced and unbalanced forces come in, and they are the key to predicting motion.

Balanced forces are forces that are equal in size but pull or push in opposite directions, so they cancel each other out. When forces are balanced, there is no overall force, and so the motion of the object does not change. Think of a book resting on a table. Gravity pulls the book down, and the table pushes the book up with exactly the same force. The two forces are balanced, so the book stays perfectly still. In a game of tug-of-war, when two evenly matched teams pull the rope in opposite directions with equal force, the rope does not move — the forces are balanced.

Unbalanced forces are forces that are not equal. When forces are unbalanced, there is an overall force — scientists call it a net force — pushing one way, and this net force changes the object's motion. The object may start moving, speed up, slow down, stop, or change direction. In that same tug-of-war, the moment one team pulls harder than the other, the forces become unbalanced and the rope suddenly moves toward the stronger team.

You can find the net force by simple adding and subtracting. If two forces push the same way, you add them together. If two forces push in opposite directions, you subtract the smaller from the larger, and the net force points in the direction of the larger force. For example, imagine two friends pushing a stuck donkey cart. Yusuf pushes forward with 100 N and Omar pushes forward with 80 N. Both push the same way, so the total forward force is 100 + 80 = 180 N. Now suppose friction pushes back against them with 150 N. The net force is 180 — 150 = 30 N forward. Because there is a leftover forward force of 30 N, the cart finally begins to roll forward.

A football is being blown by the wind. The wind pushes it to the right with a force of 12 N. A child kicks it to the left with a force of 20 N. What is the net force, and which way does the ball go?

List the forces. Wind: 12 N to the right. Kick: 20 N to the left.

The forces are in opposite directions, so subtract. 20 — 12 = 8.

Choose the direction of the larger force. The kick (20 N) is larger, so the net force points left.
concepts.example: Usually more than one force acts on an object at the same time. To predict what will happen, you must add up all the forces and see which way they win. This is where the ideas of balanced and unbalanced forces come in, and they are the key to predicting motion.

concepts.title: Measuring Forces in Newtons
concepts.explanation:
How do we actually measure the size of a force? We use a tool called a forcemeter, sometimes called a spring scale. Inside a forcemeter is a spring. When you hang a weight on the spring, the spring stretches. A small force stretches the spring only a little; a large force stretches it a lot. A scale marked in newtons beside the spring lets you read off exactly how large the force is. The market traders who weigh vegetables and fish on a hanging spring scale are using this very same idea.

The spring works because of a neat pattern: the more force you apply, the more the spring stretches, and it stretches in a steady, even way. Double the force and you double the stretch. This makes the forcemeter easy to read and reliable. In the Experiments book you will build your own forcemeter from a rubber band and a ruler, and you will use it to measure the weight of small objects around your home in newtons.

Did You Know? A medium-sized apple or mango weighs roughly 1 to 3 newtons. A 1-litre bottle of water weighs about 10 newtons. A Year 6 pupil with a mass of about 35 kg weighs around 350 newtons - that is how hard gravity pulls you toward the Earth right now.

methods.title: Build Your Own Forcemeter
methods.example: To build a simple forcemeter from a rubber band and use it to compare the weights of small objects.
steps: Tie or clip the cup to the bottom of the rubber band so it hangs down.
Hold the top of the rubber band still, or hook it over a nail or a door handle so it hangs freely.
Hold the ruler beside the rubber band. Note the starting position of the bottom of the cup when it is empty. This is your zero mark.
Place one object in the cup. Measure how far the bottom of the cup drops from the zero mark, in centimetres. Record it.
Remove the object and check the band returns to the zero mark. Then test the next object the same way.

methods.title: The Friction Ramp
methods.example: To find out how different surfaces change the amount of friction acting on a small object as it slides down a ramp.
steps: Prop up one end of the ramp on a book so it makes a gentle slope. Keep the height the same for every test — this is your fair test rule.
Lay the first surface (for example, smooth plastic) flat along the ramp.
Place your object at the top and let go without pushing. Watch whether it slides easily, slides slowly, or does not slide at all.
If it does not slide, add one more book to raise the ramp until it just begins to slide. Record how many books were needed.
Repeat with each different surface, always starting from a flat ramp and adding books one at a time.

methods.title: Racing Falling Objects (Air Resistance)
methods.example: To discover how air resistance changes the way objects fall, using two identical sheets of paper.
steps: Hold the two flat sheets of paper, one in each hand, at exactly the same height above the floor.
Drop them both at the same moment and watch how they fall. Record what you see.
Now crush one sheet tightly into a small ball. Leave the other sheet flat.
Hold both at the same height again and drop them together. Watch carefully and record which lands first.
Repeat two or three times to make sure your result is not just chance.

methods.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces Tug Test
methods.example: To feel the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces using a simple pull test.
steps: Place the small object on a smooth floor. Tie a string to each side, or hold the object gently between two fingers.
With a helper, both pull the string in opposite directions with equal, gentle force. Watch whether the object moves. Record it.
Now have one person pull a little harder than the other. Watch which way the object moves. Record it.
Try a solo version: rest a book on the table (gravity down, table up) and note that it stays still because forces are balanced.
Give the same book a gentle push so it slides and then stops. Note that an unbalanced push started it and friction stopped it.

workedExamples.title: Calculating Weight
workedExamples.prompt: Let us practise the weight rule together, one careful step at a time. Read each example slowly and make sure you understand every line before moving on. Keep the rule in front of you: Weight = mass x gravity, and on Earth gravity g = 10 N/kg.
workedExamples.solution:
Worked Example 1: The bag of rice

Amina buys a bag of rice with a mass of 5 kg in the market at Garissa. What is its weight on Earth?

Write down what you know. Mass m = 5 kg. Gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Write the rule. Weight = mass x gravity.

workedExamples.title: 1: The bag of rice
workedExamples.prompt: Amina buys a bag of rice with a mass of 5 kg in the market at Garissa. What is its weight on Earth?
workedExamples.solution:
Write down what you know. Mass m = 5 kg. Gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Write the rule. Weight = mass x gravity.

Put the numbers in. Weight = 5 x 10.

Do the multiplication. Weight = 50.

workedExamples.title: 2: The water container
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan fills a plastic jerrycan with water. The full jerrycan has a mass of 20 kg. What is its weight?
workedExamples.solution:
What you know: mass m = 20 kg, gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Rule: Weight = mass x gravity.

Substitute: Weight = 20 x 10.

Calculate: Weight = 200.

workedExamples.title: 3: Working backwards to find mass
workedExamples.prompt: Sometimes you know the weight and must find the mass. A goat weighs 300 N on Earth. What is its mass?
workedExamples.solution:
What you know: weight W = 300 N, gravity g = 10 N/kg.

Rearrange the rule. Since Weight = mass x gravity, we get mass = weight / gravity.

Substitute: mass = 300 / 10.

Calculate: mass = 30.

workedExamples.title: 4: Finding the net force
workedExamples.prompt: A football is being blown by the wind. The wind pushes it to the right with a force of 12 N. A child kicks it to the left with a force of 20 N. What is the net force, and which way does the ball go?
workedExamples.solution:
List the forces. Wind: 12 N to the right. Kick: 20 N to the left.

The forces are in opposite directions, so subtract. 20 — 12 = 8.

Choose the direction of the larger force. The kick (20 N) is larger, so the net force points left.

Answer: The net force is 8 N to the left, so the ball moves to the left.

workedExamples.title: 5: The speed of a goat
workedExamples.prompt: A goat trots 20 metres across a field in 10 seconds. What is its speed?
workedExamples.solution:
Write what you know. Distance = 20 m. Time = 10 s.

Write the rule. Speed = distance / time.

Substitute the numbers. Speed = 20 / 10.

Calculate. Speed = 2.

workedExamples.title: 6: A football on the pitch
workedExamples.prompt: Farah kicks a football and it rolls 30 metres in 6 seconds before stopping. What was its average speed?
workedExamples.solution:
What you know: distance = 30 m, time = 6 s.

Rule: Speed = distance / time.

Substitute: Speed = 30 / 6.

Calculate: Speed = 5.

workedExamples.title: 7: A journey by bus
workedExamples.prompt: A bus travels 120 kilometres from Mombasa toward Nairobi in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
workedExamples.solution:
What you know: distance = 120 km, time = 2 h.

Rule: Speed = distance / time.

Substitute: Speed = 120 / 2.

Calculate: Speed = 60.

practice.prompt: A force is best described as: (a) a colour (b) a push or a pull (c) a type of metal (d) a kind of light
practice.answer: b A force is a push or a pull. It is neither a colour, a metal, nor a kind of light.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: The unit used to measure force is the: (a) kilogram (b) metre (c) newton (d) litre
practice.answer: c Force is measured in newtons (N). Kilograms measure mass; metres measure length.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: The force that pulls a mango down toward the ground is: (a) friction (b) gravity (c) air resistance (d) tension
practice.answer: b Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward the centre of the Earth.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Mass is measured in: (a) newtons (b) kilograms (c) joules (d) seconds
practice.answer: b Mass is the amount of matter and is measured in kilograms.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: A 4 kg object on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) has a weight of: (a) 4 N (b) 14 N (c) 40 N (d) 400 N
practice.answer: c Weight = mass x gravity = 4 x 10 = 40 N.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Friction always acts: (a) in the same direction as motion (b) against the direction of motion (c) upward only (d) only in water
practice.answer: b Friction always acts against the direction of motion, slowing objects down.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Which road gives a donkey cart the most friction? (a) a smooth paved road (b) a soft sandy track (c) a wet tiled floor (d) a sheet of ice
practice.answer: b A soft sandy track grips the wheels most, giving the greatest friction.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: A parachute works because it creates a large amount of: (a) gravity (b) mass (c) air resistance (d) friction with the ground
practice.answer: c A parachute traps air and creates large air resistance to slow the fall.
practice.hint: Look back at what Weight and Mass (from weight) mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction are called: (a) unbalanced (b) balanced (c) magnetic (d) gravitational

activities.title: Build Your Own Forcemeter
activities.materials: One thin rubber band (an elastic band); A ruler or a strip of card marked in centimetres; A paper or plastic cup, or a small bag, to hold objects; String or a paper clip to hang the cup; Small objects to test: a spoon, a stone, a few coins, a small fruit such as a lime or a small mango; A pencil and notebook to record results
steps: Tie or clip the cup to the bottom of the rubber band so it hangs down.
Hold the top of the rubber band still, or hook it over a nail or a door handle so it hangs freely.
Hold the ruler beside the rubber band. Note the starting position of the bottom of the cup when it is empty. This is your zero mark.
Place one object in the cup. Measure how far the bottom of the cup drops from the zero mark, in centimetres. Record it.
Remove the object and check the band returns to the zero mark. Then test the next object the same way.
Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: The Friction Ramp
activities.materials: A flat board, a stiff book cover, or a wooden tray to use as a ramp; Some books to prop up one end of the ramp; A small object that slides, such as a coin, an eraser, or a small block; Different surface materials to lay on the ramp: a smooth plastic sheet, a piece of cloth, a sheet of rough sandpaper or a dusty mat; A ruler and a notebook
steps: Prop up one end of the ramp on a book so it makes a gentle slope. Keep the height the same for every test — this is your fair test rule.
Lay the first surface (for example, smooth plastic) flat along the ramp.
Place your object at the top and let go without pushing. Watch whether it slides easily, slides slowly, or does not slide at all.
If it does not slide, add one more book to raise the ramp until it just begins to slide. Record how many books were needed.
Repeat with each different surface, always starting from a flat ramp and adding books one at a time.

activities.title: Racing Falling Objects (Air Resistance)
activities.materials: Two identical sheets of paper of the same size; A small light object and a slightly heavier unbreakable object, such as a plastic bottle cap and a coin (optional second test); A clear space with no breakable items below; A notebook
steps: Hold the two flat sheets of paper, one in each hand, at exactly the same height above the floor.
Drop them both at the same moment and watch how they fall. Record what you see.
Now crush one sheet tightly into a small ball. Leave the other sheet flat.
Hold both at the same height again and drop them together. Watch carefully and record which lands first.
Repeat two or three times to make sure your result is not just chance.

activities.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces Tug Test
activities.materials: A length of string or a strong rubber band; A small light object such as a bottle cap or an eraser, or a toy on a smooth floor; A smooth floor or table top; A helper (a sibling, friend, or parent) for part of the test; A notebook
steps: Place the small object on a smooth floor. Tie a string to each side, or hold the object gently between two fingers.
With a helper, both pull the string in opposite directions with equal, gentle force. Watch whether the object moves. Record it.
Now have one person pull a little harder than the other. Watch which way the object moves. Record it.
Try a solo version: rest a book on the table (gravity down, table up) and note that it stays still because forces are balanced.
Give the same book a gentle push so it slides and then stops. Note that an unbalanced push started it and friction stopped it.

activities.title: Observe: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
activities.materials: One thin rubber band (an elastic band); A ruler or a strip of card marked in centimetres; A paper or plastic cup, or a small bag, to hold objects; String or a paper clip to hang the cup; Small objects to test: a spoon, a stone, a few coins, a small fruit such as a lime or a small mango; A pencil and notebook to record results
steps: Look for an example of balanced and unbalanced forces around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Weight and Mass (from weight).

rules.title: Mass and Weight Are Different
rules.text: Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kilograms and never changes. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass. It is measured in newtons and changes with gravity. A kitchen scale measures mass in kilograms. A forcemeter (spring scale) measures weight in newtons.

rules.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
rules.text: This Balanced forces mean NO change in motion. A still object stays still; a moving object keeps the same speed and direction. Unbalanced forces mean a CHANGE in motion. The object speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. It is the leftover, unbalanced part of the force — the net force — that changes how something moves.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between mass and weight. Give the correct unit for each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg), and it never changes. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons (N), and it changes with gravity.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name two forces that can slow a moving object down.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Friction and air resistance (or water resistance) both slow a moving object down. Any two of these are correct.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is friction greater on a sandy road than on a paved road?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Sand is loose and rough, so the wheels press into it and rub against many grains, creating more friction. A paved road is smooth and hard, so there is less friction.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give one example where friction is helpful and one example where friction is a nuisance.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Helpful: friction between sandals and the ground lets you walk without slipping. Nuisance: friction between machine parts makes them wear out (other sensible examples are fine).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What does it mean when we say the forces on a resting book are balanced?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: It means the downward pull of gravity and the upward push of the table are equal in size and opposite in direction, so there is no overall force and the book stays still.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe one way a force can change the shape of an object.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A force can squeeze (compress), stretch, bend, or twist an object. For example, squeezing dough or stretching a rubber band changes its shape.

rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and is measured in kilograms.

rounds.prompt: Which road gives a donkey cart the most friction?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A soft sandy track grips the wheels most, giving the greatest friction.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Net force
games.description: Practise net force through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: The tool used to measure force in newtons is a:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A forcemeter (spring scale) measures force in newtons.

rounds.prompt: The unit used to measure force is the:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N). Kilograms measure mass; metres measure length.

rounds.prompt: A 4 kg object on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) has a weight of:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Weight = mass x gravity = 4 x 10 = 40 N.

rounds.prompt: A parachute works because it creates a large amount of:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A parachute traps air and creates large air resistance to slow the fall.

games.title: Unit Champion: Speed
games.description: Practise speed through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Speed is calculated using the rule:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Speed = distance / time.

rounds.prompt: The force that pulls a mango down toward the ground is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward the centre of the Earth.

rounds.prompt: Friction always acts:
choices: in the same direction as motion
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Friction always acts against the direction of motion, slowing objects down.

rounds.prompt: Forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction are called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Equal and opposite forces are balanced forces.

selfAssessment: I can explain what a force is and describe forces as pushes or pulls that have both size and direction.
I can name the main types of force: gravity, friction, air resistance, water resistance, and pushes and pulls from contact.
I can explain the difference between mass (measured in kilograms) and weight (measured in newtons).
I can calculate the weight of an object using the rule weight = mass x gravity.
I can describe how friction helps us and how it slows us down, and compare friction on sandy and paved roads.
I can explain balanced and unbalanced forces and predict whether an object will speed up, slow down, or stay the same.
I can measure forces in newtons using a forcemeter you build yourself.
I can calculate speed using the rule speed = distance / time.
